claims.text: Nearly equiatomic five-component transition-metal HENA nanoparticles can initially form a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Random distributions of elements with disparate atomic radii produce severe local lattice distortion.
Severe local lattice distortion creates a heterogeneous potential-energy landscape that traps vacancies.
Severe local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
The lattice-distortion-induced kinetic barrier suppresses vacancy-mediated atomic diffusion.
The kinetic barrier can override the thermodynamic driving force for phase separation when configurational entropy is insufficient to stabilize the nanoscale single phase.
Atomic jumps through a severely distorted lattice have unusually high activation energies.
Sluggish diffusion kinetically arrests the alloy in a metastable single-phase state.
Kinetic trapping prevents nucleation and growth of precipitates that would otherwise be thermodynamically favored.
Kinetic limitations can decouple observed structural evolution from CALPHAD equilibrium predictions.
The HENA nanoparticles will retain a single-phase BCC structure after prolonged exposure at 600–900°C.
The HENA nanoparticles will exhibit negligible grain growth and phase separation after thermal exposure.
Comparable lower-entropy conventional alloys will undergo rapid precipitation, phase separation, or grain coarsening under the same conditions.
HENA diffusion coefficients will be orders of magnitude below values predicted by Arrhenius extrapolation from room-temperature data.
High configurational entropy can reduce the thermodynamic driving force for precipitation and stabilize a single-phase solid solution under irradiation.
Some high-entropy alloys follow conventional thermodynamic stability rules rather than exhibiting universally sluggish diffusion or entropy-controlled behavior.
For refractory systems, temperatures potentially above 1000°C may overcome the lattice-distortion-induced activation barrier.
At sufficiently large nanoparticle sizes, surface-energy effects cease to dominate and bulk thermodynamic driving forces can prevail.
Elemental combinations with similar atomic radii generate less severe lattice distortion.
Surface diffusion in nanoparticles may bypass bulk lattice-distortion-induced kinetic barriers.
